`phylosamp` now supports functionality for calculating sample sizes for
a range of common sampling objectives under periodic surveillance using
the methods described in TODO:CITATION. These objectives include
estimating a variants **growth advantage**, which captures its intrinsic
growth rate relative to other circulating variants, its **dominance
time**, or the predicted time in which the variant will reach 50%
frequency in the population, and an updated methodology for tracking the
variant's **prevalence**.
Additionally, there is a general interface to allow users to specify their own objectives
they would like to infer with variant tracking beyond these three.

#### Growth advantage

Consider a pathogen variant of interest with a growth advantage similar to the Omicron SARS-CoV-2 variant, which we conservatively specify as 0.84 per week. Suppose we are interested
in estimating the growth advantage within 8 weeks after the variant is introduced, and that there are around 10,000 confirmed cases available to sample from per week. 
Such a magnitude of confirmed cases might be appropriate for a large national surveillance system. To determine the number of sequences needed to infer the true growth advantage within 15% of its true value with 95% confidence, we may call

```{r}
vartrack_samplesize_growth(0.84, 1/10000, t=8, prob=0.95, precision=0.15)
```

Here we assume all sequences are successful and that no biases are present, yielding that **35 sequences per week** are necessary to infer this growth advantage.

To adjust for sequencing success and other biases, 
now suppose we wish to account for a 80% probability of obtaining a high-quality sequence and
that the variant has increased an increased testing sensitivity and probability of meeting
quality thresholds.
Using the same example values for these probabilities as in [Estimating bias in observed variant prevalence](V1_CoefficientDetectionBias.html) and elsewhere, we obtain a coefficient of
detection of around 1.37 and supply these settings to the calculator
```{r}
c1_c2 <- vartrack_cod_ratio(phi_v1=0.975, phi_v2=0.95, gamma_v1=0.8, gamma_v2=0.6)
vartrack_samplesize_growth(0.84, 1/10000, 8, omega=0.8, c_ratio=c1_c2)
```
Here again we have assumed the default accuracy settings of 15% precision and 95% confidence.

Within a periodic sampling framework, we can account for reporting delays between when a sample is first collected and when its results come back from sequencing. We may therefore adjust for a two week turnaround time using our previous settings as follows
```{r}
vartrack_samplesize_growth(0.84, 1/10000, 8, omega=0.8, c_ratio=c1_c2, tau=2)
```
In this example, this increases the sample size considerably since we essentially only have 6 weeks of data to work with, and hence more sequences per week are needed to fill the gap, and the variant's prevalence is lower overall within our observation window.
Since lower prevalence means the variant is more difficult to detect, more samples are required to gather the necessary information about how fast it is growing.

##### Specifying the observation period in terms of a tolerable frequency

Rather than specifying a fixed number of weeks we are willing to wait, it may be more interpretable in terms of resource planning to specify a particular prevalence we are willing to let the variant reach.
In the manuscript we refer to this value as the **observation threshold**.
A lower threshold indicates the need for more timely estimation. 
For example, we may wish to know a variant’s growth by the time it reached 30% circulation in a local population, regardless of how long it takes to reach this value.
To do so, we replace the argument `t=8` with `p_v1=0.3`, keeping our bias and turnaround time settings from the previous example
```{r}
vartrack_samplesize_growth(0.84, 1/10000, p_v1=0.3, omega=0.8, c_ratio=c1_c2, tau=2)
```
The sample size went down from the previous example since a 30% observation threshold leads to a longer observation window than 8 weeks, for these settings of `r_v1` and `p0_v1`.
We can check this as follows
```{r}
varfreq_time_logistic(p_v1=0.3, p0_v1=1/10000, r_v1=0.84)
```
Note that all sample size calculations round down the observation time when `p_v1` is specified, resulting in a conservative sample size where only "complete" time periods are used. 
Thus the previous sample size assumed 9 weeks of observation. 

#### Prevalence under periodic sampling

We now turn to estimating a variant's prevalence (frequency) under a periodic surveillance framework. Unlike with cross-sectional sampling, this allows us to account for the accrual of information over time. For example, if we want to be able to estimate the prevalence of a variant within 8 weeks of introduction, we can use all the sequences gathered in weeks 1 through 7 to begin capturing how the variant is growing over time, thus giving us a more accurate estimate of its prevalence at the 8 weeks target.

Again using our example settings for an Omicron-like variant in a nationally-sized case pool and with sampling biases modestly enriching samples for the variant of interest, the number of sequences required to estimate prevalence within 8 weeks and within 15% of the true prevalence and 95% confidence is:
```{r}
vartrack_samplesize_prev_cont(0.84, 1/10000, 8, omega=0.8, c_ratio=c1_c2)
```

For comparison, when assuming a cross-sectional surveillance setting (as might be necessary if sequences are not labelled by time, for example), the required sample size is much higher
```{r}
true_prev <- varfreq_freq_logistic(t=8, p0_v1=1/10000, r_v1=0.84)
vartrack_samplesize_prev_xsect(true_prev, prob=0.95, precision=0.15, omega=0.8)
```
Of course, with periodic surveillance sequences need to be gathered repeatedly by definition, while cross-sectional surveillance requires just a single time point.
However, in an ongoing surveillance setting sequences would ideally be collected at regular intervals 

```{r}
true_prev_pooled <- mean(varfreq_freq_logistic(t=1:8, p0_v1=1/10000, r_v1=0.84))
```
```{r}
vartrack_samplesize_prev_xsect(true_prev_pooled, prob=0.95, precision=0.15, omega=0.8)
```




<!-- Moreover, with periodic sampling, we have a nice property that sample sizes are strictly decreasing as the observation period increases. -->
<!-- This means that if $n$ sequences per week are sufficient to estimate a variant's prevalence at some time $t$, then $n$ weekly sequences are also sufficient  -->

As with the growth advantage, we can specify a observation tolerance `p_v1` rather than a fixed observation window.
